worksheet.title: Change One Block
worksheet.subtitle: Alter the code and see what happens
worksheet.learning_goal: I can change one block and tell how the result changes.

parts.title: Start with this code
parts.text: Here is Bit's base code. It starts at 1, then forward 2, then forward 1, so Bit lands on 4. In each exercise you change ONE block, find the new landing number, and tell how the change moved Bit.

parts.title: Change forward 2 to forward 3
parts.prompt: Change the forward 2 block to forward 3. Run the code. What number does Bit land on now? Did Bit land higher or lower than 4?

parts.title: Change the last block to back 1
parts.prompt: Go back to the base code. Change the last block (forward 1) to back 1. Run it. What number does Bit land on? Why is it lower?

parts.title: You try — change the start block
parts.prompt: Go back to the base code. Change start at 1 to start at 0. PREDICT the new landing number first, then run to check. How did changing the start block move every step?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Changing even one block changes what the code does. A bigger forward block lands Bit higher; a back block instead of forward lands Bit lower; a different start moves the whole code.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students alter one block of a known program at a time, find the new result, and describe how that single change affected the outcome. This is exactly C3.2 — read and alter existing code and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes — with a predict step on the last task.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor number path 0-5 so students can run the base code, then re-run after each one-block change.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: run the base code to 4. 'Now I change ONE block and see what happens.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — forward 2 → forward 3 makes 5 (one higher, one more step). Exercise 2 — last block → back 1 makes 2 (lower, Bit moves the other way).
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — start at 1 → start at 0; predict 3, then run; the whole code shifts down by one.
4. Connect: 'Each change moves Bit in a way you can describe — that is reading and altering code.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — forward 2 → forward 3: 1 → 4 → 5. Bit lands on 5, one HIGHER than 4 (one extra forward step).
Ex 2 — last block → back 1: 1 → 3 → 2. Bit lands on 2, LOWER, because a back block moves Bit the other way instead of forward.
Ex 3 — start at 0: 0 → 2 → 3. Bit lands on 3 — one lower than the base at every step because the whole code starts one number earlier.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: changing more than one block — remind students to return to the base code before each exercise (change only one thing).
Simplify: keep the base code on the floor path and physically swap one card at a time.
Extend: ask which single change to the base code would make Bit land on 1 (e.g. change forward 2 to back 2, or start at 1 → back blocks).
Success indicator: the child finds 5, 2, and 3 and explains each result in terms of the one block that changed.
